name: Mulberry

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Mulberry is about as easygoing as a fruit tree gets when it comes to soil. It does best in a deep, rich, well-drained loam, but it also grows in sandy soil and even heavy clay, and it puts up with poor, dry ground once it is established. The one thing it does not want is soil that stays wet: constant waterlogging can rot the roots. Full sun and any soil that drains is really all it asks, and a little compost worked in at planting gives a young tree a good start.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Mulberry is broadly soil-tolerant. It grows best in a deep, moist, well-drained loam but performs across sandy loams, sands, and clays, and tolerates infertile, dry, and even mildly alkaline ground once established (white mulberry in particular takes a wide pH span). The only real limit is drainage: chronically waterlogged soil invites root rot. Site it in full sun on any freely draining ground; a modest amount of organic matter at planting speeds establishment, but rich soil is not required and heavy feeding is unnecessary.

ph.note_beginner: Mulberry grows well across a wide range of soil pH and is not fussy (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is happiest around pH 6.0 to 7.0 but tolerates soil from about 5.5 up to 8.0, including the mildly alkaline soils that trouble many fruit trees. For most gardens you do not need to adjust the pH at all; just make sure the soil drains.
ph.note_seasoned: Mulberry is pH-adaptable, doing best around pH 6.0 to 7.0 but tolerating roughly 5.5 to 8.0. White mulberry in particular handles alkaline ground that stresses many stone fruits, so pH correction is rarely needed. Test before planting if in doubt, but in most soils the practical limits are drainage and sun, not pH.

fertilizer.timing: early spring as growth begins, only if growth is weak
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Mulberry is a vigorous, undemanding tree that rarely needs feeding once established; on decent soil it grows fast on its own. If a young tree is weak or the leaves pale, apply a light broadcast of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in early spring and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes rank, soft growth at the expense of fruit and can worsen bird-magnet leafiness. Never feed late in the season.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Mulberry hardly ever needs feeding. It is a fast, vigorous tree that does fine on its own in most soils. If a young tree looks weak or the leaves are pale, scatter a little balanced fertilizer around the root zone in early spring and water it in. Do not overdo it, especially with nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much just makes leafy growth instead of fruit. Do not feed late in the year.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is more than enough for the rare occasion a mulberry needs feeding. Mature trees typically need nothing; err on the side of underfeeding, since excess nitrogen (N) drives vegetative growth over fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) covers the rare time a mulberry needs feeding. Most mature trees need none at all. When in doubt, feed less, because too much nitrogen means leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: If feeding a young or weak tree, roughly 1/2 to 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age in early spring is ample, broadcast around the root zone and watered in, up to a few cups for a larger tree. Established trees on reasonable soil generally need no fertilizer at all. Do not fertilize in the planting hole; wait until growth begins.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: If a young tree needs a boost, use about 1/2 to 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of its age, spread around the roots in early spring and watered in. A grown, healthy tree usually needs no fertilizer at all. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole; wait until the tree starts growing.

companions.note_beginner: Mulberry is self-fruitful, which means one named tree makes fruit on its own with no second tree needed (a few wild seedlings are single-sex, so buy a named fruiting variety and this never comes up). Because it is a big, fast tree, the things that matter are not vegetable-garden pairings but where you put it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from a young trunk so it establishes faster, and above all keep it away from paths, patios, driveways, and parked cars, because the dropped fruit stains everything it lands on. Under the dense canopy, lawn and most plants struggle from shade and shallow roots, so plan for mulch or shade-tolerant groundcover there.
companions.note_seasoned: Mulberry is self-fruitful, so a single named tree fruits on its own without a pollinizer (a few wild seedlings are dioecious, but named cultivars sidestep that). The interactions that matter are about siting a large, vigorous tree, not classic vegetable companions: clear turf back from a young trunk to speed establishment, and site the tree well away from walkways, patios, driveways, and parking, since the abundant dropped fruit stains hard surfaces and gets tracked indoors. The dense canopy and shallow feeder roots make the ground beneath it a tough spot for lawn or bedding plants, so mulch it or use a shade-tolerant groundcover.

good_seasoned.name: Pollinator and beneficial-insect plants at the drip line
good_seasoned.label: traditional

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: General orchard-floor insectary logic. Mulberry is wind-pollinated and largely self-fruitful, so pollinator plants are not needed for fruit set; the value is diffuse habitat/beneficial support, unquantified for mulberry. traditional/low.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering herbs and pollinator plants out toward the drip line supports orchard-floor beneficials and pollinators generally. Mulberry itself is wind-pollinated and self-fruitful, so this does nothing for fruit set, but the flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that help keep the occasional whitefly or aphid in check. Keep them out toward the canopy edge rather than crowded against the trunk.

bad_seasoned.name: Walkways, patios, driveways, and parking under the canopy
bad_seasoned.label: extension_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Both UF/IFAS and NC State explicitly warn that dropped mulberry fruit stains driveways, sidewalks, patios, and cars, and advise against planting over them. extension_backed/HIGH: a direct, repeated extension siting directive.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: The single most common mulberry regret is siting. A mature tree drops enormous quantities of soft, deep-purple fruit over a long season, and it stains concrete, pavers, decking, and vehicles, then gets tracked indoors on shoes and paws. Extension guidance is explicit: do not plant a mulberry over a driveway, sidewalk, patio, or parking spot. Give it an out-of-the-way lawn or wild-edge site where the drop and the birds it draws are a feature, not a cleanup problem.

pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and near-ripe berries disappear, half-eaten fruit and purple droppings appear on the ground and on nearby surfaces, and flocks work the tree through the ripening weeks. On a large tree the loss is simply shared; on a small or netted tree it can be nearly total if not managed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Birds strip the ripe berries fast. You will see missing fruit, half-eaten berries, and purple bird droppings under and around the tree. Big flocks can show up daily while the fruit ripens.
pests.cause_seasoned: Many birds, especially catbirds, mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings, are drawn to sweet, soft mulberries and feed heavily as they ripen. This is the number-one reason home growers lose fruit, and it is a feature as much as a pest, since a mulberry is one of the best wildlife trees you can plant.
pests.cause_beginner: Lots of birds love sweet, soft mulberries and eat them as they ripen. This is the main reason people lose fruit to the tree, though it is also why a mulberry is such a great tree for attracting birds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: For a small tree, drape bird netting over it as the first berries color, and harvest ripe fruit promptly each day so less hangs available. For a large tree, netting is impractical; the traditional answer is to plant enough that there is plenty to share, and some growers deliberately keep a mulberry as a decoy to lure birds away from cherries and other prized fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: For a small tree, cover it with bird netting when the first berries start to color, and pick ripe fruit every day so there is less left for the birds. A big tree is too large to net, so the usual approach is to accept that you are sharing, or even to let the mulberry act as a decoy that keeps birds off your other fruit.
pests.prevention_seasoned: There is no way to keep birds off a large mulberry, so plan the siting and the crop around sharing: a big tree yields far more than a household can use. Net only small or dwarf trees, and pick promptly.
pests.prevention_beginner: You cannot really keep birds off a big mulberry, so plan on sharing; luckily the tree makes far more fruit than you can eat. Only bother netting small or dwarf trees, and pick ripe fruit quickly.

pests.name: Whiteflies
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny white flying insects lift off the undersides of leaves when disturbed, sometimes with sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage in a heavy infestation. Vigor is rarely affected on an established tree.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white flies rise up off the undersides of the leaves when you brush the branches, sometimes leaving a sticky film and black sooty mold below. They rarely bother an established tree much.
pests.cause_seasoned: Whiteflies (including the mulberry whitefly) are sap-feeders that colonize leaf undersides. They are a common but minor mulberry pest and mostly a cosmetic nuisance.
pests.cause_beginner: Whiteflies are small sap-sucking insects that gather under the leaves. They show up on mulberry fairly often but rarely do real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A healthy tree needs no treatment. If numbers are high on a small tree, a strong water spray to the leaf undersides or an insecticidal-soap application knocks them back; encourage the lacewings and ladybugs that prey on them.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: A healthy tree does not need treatment. On a small tree with a lot of them, spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water or insecticidal soap, and welcome the ladybugs and lacewings that eat them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which encourages the soft growth whiteflies favor. Natural predators usually keep them in balance outdoors.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy and go easy on nitrogen feeding, which draws whiteflies. Natural predators usually keep them under control outside.

pests.name: Borers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small entry holes, frass, or oozing on the trunk and larger limbs, usually on trees already stressed by drought, injury, or decline. Healthy, vigorous mulberries are seldom attacked.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small holes, sawdust-like frass, or oozing on the trunk or big branches, mostly on trees that are already stressed or damaged. A healthy tree is rarely bothered.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several wood-boring beetle and moth larvae can attack mulberry, but almost always as a secondary problem on trees weakened by drought stress, mechanical wounds, or age. Borers follow decline rather than cause it in a healthy tree.
pests.cause_beginner: A few kinds of borer (beetle and moth larvae) can get into mulberry, but usually only when the tree is already weak from drought, wounds, or old age. They tend to follow trouble rather than start it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: The durable control is tree health: water through droughts, avoid trunk wounds from mowers and trimmers, and prune out and destroy any dead or infested wood. There is no practical rescue spray for larvae already tunneling inside.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The best fix is a healthy tree: water it in droughts, keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk, and cut out and destroy any dead or infested branches. Once larvae are inside the wood, no spray reaches them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and unwounded. A well-sited, adequately watered mulberry rarely gives borers an opening.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy and avoid wounding the trunk. A well-placed, watered mulberry rarely has borer trouble.

diseases.name: Popcorn disease
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Some berries on the tree swell up abnormally, with individual segments (carpels) enlarging and staying hard and greenish, so the fruit looks like a little cluster of popcorn kernels instead of a normal soft berry. Affected fruit does not ripen properly and clings to the tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Some berries grow oddly, with the little segments puffing up hard and greenish so the fruit looks like tiny popcorn instead of a soft berry. Those berries never ripen right and hang on the tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Popcorn disease is caused by the fungus Ciboria carunculoides, which infects the developing fruit and turns the carpels into hard sclerotia. It is largely a southern problem, and white mulberries and their hybrids are the most susceptible; it is usually of minor importance but can cause real fruit loss on trees grown for eating.
diseases.cause_beginner: Popcorn disease is a fungus (Ciboria carunculoides) that gets into the developing fruit and makes it swell into hard, popcorn-like lumps. It mostly shows up in the South, and white mulberries and hybrids catch it most. It is usually minor but can cost you fruit on a tree you grow for eating.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home spray that cures it. Control is sanitation: as the disease appears, remove and destroy the affected fruit on the tree and rake up and bury or discard fallen fruit and debris beneath it, since that is where the fungus overwinters to reinfect next year.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: No home spray fixes it. The control is cleanup: pick off and throw away the affected berries, and rake up and bury or bin the fallen fruit under the tree, because that is where the fungus waits out the winter to come back next year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Year-round sanitation is the prevention: clear fallen and mummified fruit each season so the fungus has nowhere to overwinter. Where popcorn disease is a known local problem, favor red mulberry or a more resistant hybrid over the most susceptible white types.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen fruit each year so the fungus cannot overwinter. If popcorn disease is common in your area, choose a red mulberry or a tougher hybrid rather than the most susceptible white types.

diseases.name: Bacterial blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular, water-soaked spots appear on the leaves and turn dark, and young shoots can show black streaks or stripes; badly hit shoot tips may die back. Damage is usually cosmetic on an established tree and worst in wet springs.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get angular, water-soaked spots that turn dark, and new shoots can have black streaks; bad cases kill the shoot tips. It usually just looks bad rather than harming an established tree, and it is worst in wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Bacterial blight is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori, which spreads in cool, wet spring weather and enters young tissue. It is a minor mulberry disease that flares in wet seasons and rarely threatens a healthy tree.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacterial blight is a bacterium (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) that spreads in cool, wet spring weather and infects new growth. It is a minor disease that shows up in wet years and rarely hurts a healthy tree.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy blackened, blighted shoots during dry weather to remove the bacterial source, and avoid overhead watering that keeps foliage wet. No spray is warranted on a home tree beyond this sanitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out and throw away the blackened, blighted shoots in dry weather, and avoid watering over the top of the tree so the leaves stay drier. On a backyard tree, that cleanup is all that is needed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep the canopy open and the foliage dry, prune only in dry weather, and remove infected wood promptly. A vigorous, well-spaced tree shrugs off the disease in most years.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree open so air moves through it, prune only when it is dry, and remove any infected shoots. A healthy, well-spaced tree easily shrugs this off most years.

diseases.name: Leaf spots and minor foliar diseases
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Scattered fungal leaf spots, or whitish patches (false mildew and powdery mildew) on leaf undersides in mid to late summer, sometimes with modest leaf drop on older trees in a wet season. Vigor and cropping are rarely affected.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Spots on the leaves, or whitish patches underneath them in late summer, sometimes with a few leaves dropping in a wet year. It rarely affects how the tree grows or fruits.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A group of minor leaf fungi (Cercospora and Cercosporella leaf spots, false mildew, and powdery mildews) can spot or coat mulberry foliage, mostly late in the season and mostly in wet weather. On mulberry these are cosmetic and seldom worth treating.
diseases.cause_beginner: A few minor leaf fungi (leaf spots and mildews) can mark mulberry leaves, mostly late in the season and in wet weather. On mulberry they are just cosmetic and rarely worth doing anything about.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment is needed on a healthy tree. Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn to reduce carryover, and keep the canopy open for airflow. Fungicides are reserved for prized specimens with a serious recurring problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A healthy tree needs no treatment. Rake up and remove fallen leaves in fall to cut down on next year's spores, and keep the tree open so air flows through. Sprays are only for special trees with a bad, repeated problem.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Open-canopy pruning, autumn leaf cleanup, and good air movement are the whole prevention program. Well-grown mulberries carry these diseases without meaningful harm.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keeping the tree open, cleaning up fallen leaves in fall, and letting air move through are all you need. A well-grown mulberry carries these without real harm.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water regularly through the first one to two seasons to establish the roots, roughly weekly in the absence of rain. After that, mulberry is notably drought-tolerant and an established tree rarely needs irrigation, though watering through the final weeks of fruit sizing improves size and sweetness. Cut back sharply in winter dormancy.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water a new mulberry regularly for its first year or two, about once a week when it does not rain, so the roots get going. After that it is very drought-tolerant and an older tree seldom needs watering, though a good soak while the berries are filling makes them bigger and sweeter. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs almost none.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root depth rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 5 gallons per soak; a bearing tree that is watered at all wants the rough equivalent of an inch per week during fruit fill in dry spells. Deep, infrequent soaks build the deep roots that carry mulberry through drought.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older tree needs little, but a deep weekly soak while the fruit is filling, if the weather is dry, pays off in better berries. Deep soaks grow deep, drought-proof roots.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip, soaker, or a slow hose out toward the drip line, keeping the trunk base itself uncrowded. Overhead watering is not the concern it is with stone fruit, but soil that drains freely between waterings matters most, since mulberry dislikes standing water far more than dryness.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line, soaker hose, or a slow trickle from a hose, spreading it out toward the edge of the branches. The main thing is that the soil drains between waterings; mulberry hates sitting in water much more than it minds being dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Overwatering or poor drainage shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and a stalled or declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate. Because mulberry is so drought-adapted, chronic wet feet is a far more common cause of trouble than dryness; soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellow leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that just sits there or goes downhill. Since mulberry handles dry soil so well, staying too wet is the bigger risk. Soil that never dries out is your cue to back off.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, and early leaf drop in a prolonged drought, and on the fruit as poor sizing during the fill period. An established mulberry tolerates real dry stress and usually recovers, but berries sized under drought stay small; the tree itself is rarely lost to dryness.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, and some early leaf drop in a long dry spell, and smaller berries if it runs dry while the fruit is filling. An established mulberry shrugs off dry spells and usually bounces back; the tree itself is rarely killed by drought.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil evenly moist, never waterlogged. A deep soak of about 5 gallons weekly, adjusted for rain and heat, builds the deep root system mulberry relies on to shrug off later droughts.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the tree is settling in, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots that make it so drought-tough later.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: During fruit fill, a bearing tree in a dry spell benefits from the equivalent of about an inch of water per week as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates into larger, sweeter berries; an established tree with regular rain needs nothing extra.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the berries are filling, an older tree in a dry spell does better with about an inch of water a week as deep soaks. Steady water now means bigger, sweeter fruit. If it is raining regularly, you do not need to add any.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely on rainfall and water only in a prolonged dry winter. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs almost no water. Let rain do the work and water only during a long dry winter stretch. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone to encourage deep rooting; free drainage between waterings matters more than frequency, since mulberry is drought-adapted but intolerant of standing water. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first season or two to establish; mature trees are strongly drought-tolerant and often need no irrigation at all.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give a deep soak now and then at the ground rather than a little every day, and make sure the soil drains between waterings. Mulberry handles dry soil far better than wet. Young trees need steady water for the first year or two to get established; after that, an older tree can often go without watering entirely.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The one window where watering clearly pays off is fruit fill, the couple of weeks as berries size and sweeten; a bearing tree kept watered then, in a dry spell, sizes better fruit. Establishment (the first season or two) is the other sensitive period. Outside those, an established mulberry is remarkably self-sufficient.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The time watering matters most is while the berries are sizing up, when a good soak in a dry spell makes them bigger and sweeter. The other important stretch is the first season or two while the tree gets established. Apart from those, an older mulberry mostly takes care of itself.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Mulberries are extremely perishable and do not hold at room temperature; ripe fruit begins to soften and ferment within a day. Eat them the day they are picked, or refrigerate immediately. They also stain hands, cloth, and counters, so handle over a bowl.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Mulberries do not keep on the counter. Ripe fruit gets soft and starts to spoil within a day, so eat them the day you pick them or put them in the fridge right away. They stain everything, so work over a bowl.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate ripe mulberries unwashed in a shallow, breathable container and use within 2 to 3 days; washing before storage hastens breakdown. Their very short shelf life (and how poorly they pack and ship) is exactly why mulberries are a home-grown and farmers-market fruit, rarely a grocery one.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep ripe mulberries in the fridge, unwashed, in a shallow open container, and eat them within 2 to 3 days (wash them only right before eating). They spoil fast and bruise easily, which is why you almost never see them in a grocery store; a mulberry is a fruit you grow or pick yourself.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Mulberries freeze very well. Rinse gently, drain and pat dry, freeze in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags. Frozen berries keep for many months and are excellent for baking, jam, syrup, and smoothies. Freezing is the practical way to handle a heavy crop that ripens faster than you can eat it fresh.
storage.freezer_beginner: Mulberries freeze really well, which is the best way to deal with a big crop. Rinse them gently, drain and pat dry, spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for months and are great for baking, jam, syrup, and smoothies.
storage.notes_seasoned: Because tree-ripe mulberries last only days and stain readily, plan for the crop: pick into shallow containers, refrigerate or freeze promptly, and turn a heavy flush into jam, syrup, or the freezer rather than letting it drop and stain the ground.
storage.notes_beginner: Ripe mulberries only last a couple of days and stain easily, so have a plan for them: pick into shallow containers, chill or freeze them right away, and turn a big pick into jam, syrup, or frozen bags instead of letting them drop and stain the ground.

recommended.name: Illinois Everbearing
recommended.recommended_note: The standard hardy backyard mulberry (Morus alba x rubra). Self-fruitful, very cold-hardy (to about -20°F, zones 4 to 9), with large sweet berries that ripen over an extended summer window. A reliable first mulberry for most of the country.

recommended.name: Dwarf Everbearing
recommended.recommended_note: A naturally dwarf, low-chill, self-fruitful mulberry that stays small and fruits young, even the first year and in a large container. The pick for small yards, patios, and mild-winter areas.

recommended.name: Silk Hope
recommended.recommended_note: A vigorous Morus alba x rubra hybrid (zones 5 to 9) with large sweet black fruit over about two months in early summer, and better resistance to Southeastern fungal problems than Illinois Everbearing.

recommended.name: Pakistan
recommended.recommended_note: A long-fruited, low-chill mulberry for warm regions (roughly zones 7 to 10), bearing very long, firm, sweet-tart berries. Best in the South, warm California, and low deserts; not cold-hardy in the North.

recommended.name: Black Beauty
recommended.recommended_note: A compact black mulberry (Morus nigra type, roughly zones 7 to 10) prized for rich, intense flavor. Smaller and slower than the vigorous hybrids, well suited to small warm-climate gardens and large containers.

recommended.name: Oscar
recommended.recommended_note: A vigorous, very heavy-bearing Morus alba x nigra type for warm and mild regions, with large juicy berries over a long season. A productive choice where winters are mild.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose a mulberry first by climate and size, then by fruit. For cold winters, pick a hardy hybrid such as Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope (zones 4 to 5 and up); for mild and warm regions, low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, and Oscar shine. For a small space or a container, choose a genuine dwarf such as Dwarf Everbearing. Nearly all named fruiting cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, so a single tree bears; the caveat is to buy a NAMED fruiting cultivar rather than an unnamed seedling, since a few wild seedlings are single-sex.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a mulberry first by your climate and how big a tree you want, then by the fruit. For cold winters, choose a hardy hybrid like Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope; for warm areas, low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, or Oscar do great. For a small yard or a pot, choose a real dwarf like Dwarf Everbearing. Almost all named fruiting varieties fruit on their own, so one tree is enough. The one rule is to buy a NAMED fruiting variety, not an unnamed seedling, because a few wild seedlings turn out to be male and never fruit.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to mulberry. It is planted as a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring, or as a container tree, not raised from a tender indoor seedling, so there is no soft transplant to acclimate.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoors) does not apply to mulberry. You plant it as a dormant bare-root tree in late winter or early spring, or from a pot, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring before bud break, once the ground can be worked; container trees can go in through the growing season with attentive watering. Soak bare roots for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree at the depth it grew in the nursery; if it is grafted, keep the graft union above the soil line. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and keep the surrounding area weed-free and mulched. Give it room: a standard mulberry is a large, spreading tree.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug; a potted tree can go in during the growing season if you keep it watered. Soak bare roots in water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out, and set the tree at the same depth it grew before (if it is a grafted tree, keep the graft bump above the soil). Fill in with the soil you dug out, water it in well, and keep the area around it weed-free and mulched. Give it plenty of space, because a standard mulberry gets big.

soil_mix.type_beginner: If you grow a dwarf mulberry in a pot, use a chunky, free-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peaty potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix with perlite or pumice drains well. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains poorly when watered often.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Aim for drainage. If the mix holds water, stir in more perlite or pumice, and top it with a thin layer of compost rather than mixing lots of rich material through the pot. Avoid water-holding crystals and heavy peat.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: For a dwarf or weeping mulberry in a container, use a coarse, free-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity roots need; skip native garden soil, which compacts under frequent irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Keep amendments drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin compost layer rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive additives, which work against the freely draining root zone mulberry wants.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A potted mulberry dries out much faster than one in the ground, so check it often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. It still hates sitting in water, so never leave the pot in a full saucer. In winter, when the tree is resting, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed lightly with a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the tree does not push tender growth into fall. Do not feed at planting, and stop once the tree drops its leaves.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold reaches the soil from every side. A mulberry that is hardy in your yard can still have its roots freeze in a pot. Before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed or move it into an unheated but sheltered spot like a garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. It still needs the cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm room.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Roots in a container sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, so a mulberry hardy in your soil may still freeze its roots in a pot. Before hard freezes, sink the pot to its rim in a bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space (garage or shed) that holds dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots. It still needs its winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: A standard mulberry is far too large and vigorous for a pot, so container growing means choosing a naturally dwarf or weeping variety like Dwarf Everbearing, which is bred for it and even fruits young in a pot. In a big, well-draining container it can be a productive patio tree, but plan on regular watering, occasional root pruning, and winter protection of the pot. For the everyday full-size mulberry, plant it in the ground.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: A standard mulberry is far too large and vigorous for containers, so container culture means starting with a genetic-dwarf or weeping cultivar (Dwarf Everbearing and similar), which are bred for pots and bear young. Given the largest practical, freely draining pot, such a tree makes a productive patio specimen, but expect regular watering, periodic root pruning to hold size, and winter root protection. For the ordinary full-size mulberry, in-ground is the only sensible choice.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted mulberry dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. It still resents standing water, so never leave the pot in a full saucer. Through dormancy it needs only enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often rather than in one heavy dose: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into frost. Do not feed at planting, and ease off once the tree goes dormant.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is a poor match for mulberry. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously moist, and mulberry's one real intolerance is standing water at the roots. Use a pot that drains freely and let the mix dry between waterings, rather than a constant water table held against the roots.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not a good choice for mulberry. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and wet roots are the one thing mulberry really dislikes. Use a pot that drains freely and let the soil dry out a bit between waterings.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Cold protection in a pot covers more than the roots: an exposed trunk and, on a grafted tree, the graft union are also vulnerable to freeze. Wrap or shade the lower trunk in exposed sites and bank mulch or sink the pot to insulate the roots. Aim for a cold, stable dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots; a too-warm shelter that breaks dormancy early is its own hazard.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Protecting a potted mulberry in winter is about more than the roots. The bare trunk, and the graft bump on a grafted tree, can also be hurt by freezing. In exposed spots wrap or shade the lower trunk, and pile mulch around a sunk pot to insulate the roots. You want a cold, steady rest without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots, and be careful that a too-warm spot can wake the tree early.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a mulberry: it is a permanent tree that holds its site for decades. Mulberry has no notable replant-disease problem the way stone fruit does, so it can follow most previous plantings, but choose the site carefully for the long term, since a mature tree is hard to move and the fruit drop dictates placement.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a mulberry the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays put for decades. Unlike peaches, mulberry has no special replant problem, so it can follow most things. The main thing is to pick the right spot from the start, away from paths and patios, because a big tree is hard to move.
rotation.good_after: any well-drained, full-sun site with room for a large tree, away from paths, patios, and drives
rotation.note_seasoned: Site selection, not rotation, is the real decision for a mulberry: full sun, free drainage, plenty of room for a large spreading tree, and well clear of hard surfaces the fruit would stain. There is no rotation interval to observe.
rotation.note_beginner: For a mulberry, choosing the spot matters far more than rotation. Give it full sun, soil that drains, lots of room, and keep it away from anything the fruit could stain. There is no rotation schedule to follow.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root or container)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring for a bare-root tree, while dormant and the ground can be worked; a container tree can go in through the growing season.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring for a bare-root tree, while it is leafless and the ground can be dug; a potted tree can go in during the growing season.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root whip with firm buds and healthy roots, or a leafy container tree. If it is grafted, find the graft union low on the trunk and keep it above the soil.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young tree with firm buds and good roots, or a potted tree. If it is grafted, there is a bump low on the trunk (the graft) to keep above the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig a hole as wide as the roots spread and no deeper than they grew before, set the tree at that depth, backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch a weed-free circle. Give it plenty of room; a standard mulberry gets large.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Dig a wide hole no deeper than the roots grew before, set the tree at that depth, fill in with the soil you dug out, water it in well, and mulch a weed-free circle. Leave lots of room, because a standard mulberry gets big.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date, the cultivar, and whether it is on its own roots or grafted.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted and which mulberry variety it is.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid new shoot growth, since mulberry establishes fast. The root system is settling in and any light fruiting should be secondary to growth.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fast new growth, because mulberry gets going quickly. The roots are settling in, and growing well matters more than fruit this year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly through the first season so the roots establish, keep a weed-free mulched circle around the trunk (mulch off the bark), and begin light shaping if needed. Little else is required; mulberry is undemanding.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water regularly this first season so the roots get going, keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk (mulch off the bark), and do a little light shaping if needed. There is not much else to do; mulberry is easy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and any early shaping.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and any light pruning.

growth_stages.name: Framework and light training (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first few years, establishing a sound branch framework before the tree is large.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first few years, while you set up the main branches before the tree gets big.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A fast-growing young tree building its shape. Mulberry needs far less structural pruning than stone fruit; the aim is a strong, open framework and a manageable height.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A fast-growing young tree taking shape. Mulberry needs much less pruning than a peach; you just want strong main branches and a height you can reach.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: In dormancy, remove crossing, weak, or badly placed shoots and head the tree to a reachable height if you want to keep it low for easier harvest. Keep cuts modest; mulberry bleeds sap heavily if cut when active.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In winter, cut out branches that cross or are weak or badly placed, and shorten the tree to a height you can pick from if you want it low. Keep pruning light and do it while the tree is dormant, because mulberry bleeds a lot of sap if cut while it is growing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each dormant-season shaping and any height-reduction cuts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune each winter and any cuts to lower the tree.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the bare winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless tree at rest. Mulberry has a modest chill requirement compared with stone fruit, so even mild-winter areas usually satisfy it. There is little to see.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting tree. Mulberry needs less winter cold than a peach, so most areas give it enough. There is not much to see.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required. This is the window for any structural or size-reduction pruning (done now to avoid heavy sap bleeding) and for clearing fallen fruit and debris that could carry disease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do. This is the time for any shaping or size-reduction pruning (do it now so the tree does not bleed sap), and for clearing fallen fruit and debris that could carry disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the dormant pruning date and any winter cleanup.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned and any winter cleanup.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Deep dormancy, roughly January into February, well before the sap rises.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Deep winter, around January into February, before the sap starts to move.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches that show the tree's structure. This is the only safe pruning window, since mulberry bleeds copiously if cut once growth begins.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the shape. This is the safe time to prune, because mulberry oozes a lot of sap if you cut it after it starts growing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune in deep dormancy: remove dead, diseased, crossing, and crowding wood, and reduce height if desired for easier picking. Mulberry needs only light annual pruning, far less than stone fruit; make clean cuts and avoid large wounds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune in deep winter: cut out dead, diseased, crossing, or crowded branches, and lower the height if you want easier picking. Mulberry needs only light pruning each year, much less than a peach. Make clean cuts and avoid big wounds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the dormant pruning date and how much you removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned and how much you took off.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Spring, as the tree leafs out; timing shifts by region from late winter in the warm South to spring in the North.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Spring, as the leaves come out; earlier in warm areas, later in cold ones.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small, greenish catkins rather than showy flowers. Mulberry is wind-pollinated and self-fruitful, so a single named tree sets fruit on its own; there is little to do at bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small greenish flower clusters (catkins), not showy blooms. Mulberry pollinates by wind and fruits on its own, so one named tree sets fruit by itself and there is little to do.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Simply let the tree set its crop. In the coldest zones, watch for a hard late frost on newly emerging growth, though mulberry blooms later and is far less frost-vulnerable at bloom than stone fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Just let the tree set its fruit. In the coldest areas, keep an eye out for a hard late frost on the new growth, though mulberry blooms later and is much less frost-sensitive at bloom than a peach.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record when bloom and leaf-out began.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the tree bloomed and leafed out.

growth_stages.name: Fruit development
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Spring into summer, as the berries form and swell over several weeks.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Spring into summer, as the berries form and grow over several weeks.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green berries forming along the shoots and slowly coloring to red then deep purple-black. Mulberry does NOT need thinning; the tree carries and ripens a heavy crop over an extended window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Green berries forming along the branches and slowly turning red then dark purple-black. Mulberry does not need thinning; the tree ripens a big crop over a long stretch.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep a bearing tree watered through fruit fill in dry spells for better size and sweetness, and get bird netting ready for a small tree as the first berries color. No thinning is needed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Give a bearing tree a good soak during dry spells while the berries fill, for bigger, sweeter fruit, and have bird netting ready for a small tree as the berries start to color. There is no thinning to do.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record when fruit set and began coloring.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the berries formed and started to color.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring to summer, ripening over several weeks; earlier in the South, later in the North.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring to summer, ripening over several weeks; earlier in warm areas, later in cold ones.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Berries at full deep purple-black (or their ripe cultivar color) that detach with the gentlest touch and are soft and sweet. A mulberry ripens a little at a time over weeks, so it is picked repeatedly, and ripe fruit drops readily.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Berries at full dark color that come off with the lightest touch and are soft and sweet. A mulberry ripens a bit at a time over weeks, so you pick it again and again, and ripe fruit falls easily.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick ripe berries every day or two, or spread a sheet and gently shake the branches to collect the drop. Handle over containers, since they stain, and refrigerate or freeze promptly. Clear fallen fruit so it does not stain or draw pests.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick ripe berries every day or two, or lay a sheet under the tree and gently shake the branches to catch the drop. Work over a bowl, because they stain, and chill or freeze them right away. Clean up fallen fruit so it does not stain the ground or draw pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked and roughly how much you got.

notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root tree now while it is leafless and the ground is workable, or plant a container tree. Choose a full-sun, freely draining site with plenty of room, and, above all, well clear of walkways, patios, and drives the fruit would stain. If it is grafted, keep the graft union above the soil line.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a bare-root mulberry while it is leafless and the ground can be dug, or to plant a potted one. Pick a sunny, well-draining spot with lots of room, and keep it well away from paths, patios, and driveways the fruit could stain. If it is grafted, keep the graft bump above the soil.

notifications.body_seasoned: If the tree needs shaping, prune now in deep dormancy. Mulberry bleeds sap heavily if cut once growth resumes, so winter is the only safe window. Keep it light: remove dead, crossing, and crowding wood and reduce height if you want easier picking.
notifications.body_beginner: If the tree needs shaping, prune now while it is deep in its winter rest. Mulberry oozes a lot of sap if cut after it wakes up, so winter is the safe time. Keep it light: take out dead, crossing, or crowded branches and lower the height if you want.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first season, keep a young mulberry watered so the roots establish, roughly weekly without rain. It grows fast and becomes very drought-tolerant once established, so this early watering is the main care it needs.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first season, keep a young mulberry watered so the roots get going, about once a week when it does not rain. It grows fast and becomes very drought-tough once established, so this early watering is most of the care it needs.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your mulberry is leafing out and setting its inconspicuous catkins. It is self-fruitful and wind-pollinated, so a single named tree fruits on its own with no partner needed. In the coldest zones, watch for a hard late frost on tender new growth.
notifications.body_beginner: Your mulberry is leafing out and making its small flower clusters. It fruits on its own by wind, so one named tree needs no partner. In the coldest areas, watch for a hard late frost on the new growth.

notifications.title_seasoned: Berries are coloring, plan for birds
notifications.title_beginner: Berries are coloring, watch the birds
notifications.body_seasoned: As the first berries color, birds will move in fast. Net a small tree now if you want the crop, and plan to pick ripe fruit daily. A large tree cannot be netted, so plan to share; a mulberry is a top wildlife tree.
notifications.body_beginner: As the first berries color, birds will show up fast. Cover a small tree with netting now if you want the fruit, and plan to pick ripe berries every day. A big tree is too large to net, so plan on sharing; a mulberry is a great tree for birds.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to pick, and keep picking
notifications.body_seasoned: Mulberries ripen a little at a time over several weeks and are extremely perishable, so pick every day or two, or shake the branches onto a sheet. Handle over containers since they stain, and refrigerate or freeze promptly. Clear fallen fruit as you go.
notifications.body_beginner: Mulberries ripen a bit at a time over several weeks and spoil fast, so pick every day or two, or shake the branches onto a sheet. Work over a bowl because they stain, and chill or freeze them right away. Clean up fallen fruit as you go.

notifications.body_seasoned: As the leaves fall, rake up fallen fruit and leaves under the tree. This is the cheapest disease control: it removes the overwintering source of popcorn disease and minor leaf diseases, and keeps the drop from staining and drawing pests.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves drop, rake up the fallen fruit and leaves under the tree. This is the easiest way to prevent disease, since it clears where popcorn disease and leaf diseases wait out the winter, and keeps the drop from staining or drawing pests.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the mulberry?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off: note when bloom and harvest landed this year, clear any fallen fruit, and scan the trunk for wounds. Logging the dates now makes the tree's rhythm clearer over time.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look is worth it: jot down when the tree bloomed and when you picked, clear any fallen fruit, and check the trunk for wounds. Writing the dates down helps you see the tree's rhythm year to year.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: In the coldest zones, a hard late frost can nip newly emerging leaves and shoots. Mulberry blooms later and is far less frost-vulnerable than stone fruit, and it usually pushes new growth to recover, but a small tree can be covered overnight if a hard freeze is forecast on tender growth.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In the coldest areas, a hard late frost can burn the new leaves and shoots. Mulberry leafs out later and handles frost much better than a peach, and it usually grows back, but you can cover a small tree overnight if a hard freeze is coming while the growth is tender.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain while fruit is ripe
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heavy rain on ripe mulberries knocks fruit down and can split and sour it on the tree, and a wet canopy favors minor leaf diseases. After a soaking rain, pick or shake down any ripe fruit promptly rather than leaving it to spoil, and clear the drop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Heavy rain on ripe mulberries knocks fruit down and can split and spoil it on the tree, and wet leaves invite minor leaf diseases. After a heavy rain, pick or shake down the ripe fruit rather than leaving it to rot, and clean up what dropped.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry stretch: water young trees and fruit fill
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell: water new trees and ripening fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Mulberry is strongly drought-tolerant once established, so a mature tree usually needs nothing. The two windows where a deep soak still pays off are a first-year tree putting down roots and a bearing tree during fruit fill, when dryness leaves the berries small.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: An established mulberry handles drought well, so a grown tree usually needs nothing. The two times a deep soak still helps are a first-year tree getting its roots down and a fruiting tree while the berries fill, when dryness makes them small.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Mulberry takes heat very well and is a good choice for hot climates. In an extreme, prolonged heat spell, leaf margins can scorch (summer scorch) if the soil is also dry, so keep an establishing or bearing tree watered; a mature tree usually rides out heat unbothered.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Mulberry handles heat very well and is a good tree for hot places. In an extreme, long heat wave the leaf edges can scorch if the soil is also dry, so keep a young or fruiting tree watered; a grown tree usually shrugs off the heat.

planting.text_seasoned: Site the tree well away from walkways, patios, driveways, and parking. The abundant dropped fruit stains hard surfaces and tracks indoors; this is the most common mulberry regret.
planting.text_beginner: Plant well away from paths, patios, driveways, and where cars park. The dropped fruit stains everything and gets tracked inside, which is the thing people most wish they had thought about.
planting.author: claude_code_gs_arc

planting.text_seasoned: Give a standard mulberry room: it is a large, fast, spreading tree. Plant in full sun on freely draining ground, or choose a dwarf or weeping cultivar for a small space.
planting.text_beginner: Give a standard mulberry plenty of space, because it grows into a big, fast, wide tree. Plant in full sun where the soil drains, or pick a dwarf or weeping type for a small yard.
planting.author: claude_code_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: Water regularly through the first season so roots establish; after that, mulberry is strongly drought-tolerant and rarely needs irrigation.
establishment.text_beginner: Water regularly the first season so the roots get going. After that mulberry is very drought-tough and hardly needs watering.
establishment.author: claude_code_gs_arc

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Head a young tree to a reachable height early if you want easy picking; mulberry tolerates hard shaping while young and needs far less structural pruning than stone fruit.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: If you want to pick easily, shorten the young tree to a reachable height early. Mulberry takes hard shaping while young and needs much less pruning than a peach.
scaffold_formation.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Do any pruning in deep dormancy. Mulberry bleeds sap heavily if cut once growth resumes, so winter is the safe window.
dormancy.text_beginner: Do any pruning in the depth of winter. Mulberry oozes a lot of sap if you cut it after it wakes up, so winter is the safe time.
dormancy.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Keep pruning light: remove dead, crossing, and crowding wood and reduce height if desired. Mulberry fruits without the hard annual renewal stone fruit demands.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune lightly: take out dead, crossing, or crowded branches and lower the height if you like. Mulberry fruits fine without the hard yearly pruning a peach needs.
dormant_prune.author: claude_code_gs_arc

blossom.text_seasoned: A single named mulberry fruits on its own. It is self-fruitful and wind-pollinated, and many cultivars set fruit parthenocarpically, so no second tree or pollinator is needed.
blossom.text_beginner: One named mulberry fruits by itself. It is self-fruitful and pollinated by wind, and many types even set fruit without any pollination, so you do not need a second tree.
blossom.author: claude_code_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Do not thin mulberry; the tree ripens its whole crop over weeks. Get bird netting ready for a small tree as the first berries color.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Do not thin a mulberry; it ripens all its fruit over several weeks. Have bird netting ready for a small tree as the first berries start to color.
fruit_set.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Ripe mulberries are extremely perishable and detach at a touch. Pick every day or two, or shake the branches onto a sheet, and refrigerate or freeze promptly.
harvest.text_beginner: Ripe mulberries spoil fast and fall at a touch. Pick every day or two, or shake the branches onto a sheet, and chill or freeze them right away.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Expect to share with birds and to manage the drop. A mature tree yields more than a household can use, so freeze the surplus and clear fallen fruit so it does not stain or draw pests.
harvest.text_beginner: Plan on sharing with birds and dealing with the drop. A grown tree makes more than you can eat, so freeze the extra and clean up fallen fruit so it does not stain the ground or draw pests.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard mulberry is an extraordinarily heavy bearer, commonly yielding many gallons of fruit, on the order of tens of pounds and often far more than a household can use, ripening over several weeks. Yield is limited mainly by tree size and birds, not by feeding or thinning; the practical constraint is picking and using the crop, not growing it.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown mulberry produces a huge amount of fruit, easily many gallons over several weeks, usually far more than one family can eat. How much you get depends mostly on the size of the tree and how much the birds take, not on feeding or thinning. The hard part is picking and using it all, not growing it.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach heavy bearing within a few years and stay productive for decades, given only light annual pruning. A named everbearing cultivar spreads its crop over a long window; a standard tree simply overwhelms with fruit at peak.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A mulberry reaches heavy production within a few years and keeps bearing for decades with only light pruning. Everbearing types spread the fruit over a long stretch; a full-size tree just gives you an overwhelming amount at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little to no fruit in the first year or two while the tree establishes. Some named everbearing cultivars set a light crop early, sometimes even the first year, but real production begins around years 2 to 3 and builds from there.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much fruit the first year or two while the tree settles in. Some everbearing varieties give a little early, sometimes even the first year, but real crops start around years 2 to 3 and grow from there.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing mulberry planting or care by lunar phase; site, drainage, and cultivar choice govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree grows well but sets no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree is healthy but gives no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree is vigorous but never fruits. The usual causes are a young tree not yet of bearing age (mulberry typically starts around years 2 to 3), a fruitless ornamental mulberry (some are sold specifically as non-fruiting shade trees), or, less commonly, a single-sex seedling, since a few wild mulberries are dioecious with male and female flowers on separate trees. Named fruiting cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, so a lone one fruits on its own. The fix is the plant, not the care: buy a named FRUITING cultivar (not a fruitless ornamental), and give a young tree a couple more seasons.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree grows fine but never fruits. Usually it is just young (mulberry starts fruiting around years 2 to 3), or it is a fruitless ornamental mulberry sold as a no-fruit shade tree, or, less often, a wild seedling that happens to be male, since a few mulberries have separate male and female trees. Named fruiting varieties fruit on their own. The fix is the plant, not how you care for it: buy a named FRUITING variety, and give a young tree another year or two.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Buy a named self-fruitful FRUITING cultivar (Illinois Everbearing, Dwarf Everbearing, and similar), avoid fruitless ornamentals, and be patient with a young tree.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Buy a named self-fruitful FRUITING variety like Illinois Everbearing or Dwarf Everbearing, avoid the fruitless ornamental kinds, and give a young tree time.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Berries swell into hard, greenish popcorn-like lumps
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Berries turn into hard popcorn-like lumps
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Some berries swell abnormally, with segments enlarging and staying hard and greenish so the fruit looks like popcorn, and they never ripen. This is popcorn disease, the fungus Ciboria carunculoides, most common in the South and on white mulberries and their hybrids. There is no home spray; it is managed by sanitation. Remove and destroy affected fruit and clear the fallen fruit and debris beneath the tree, since that is where the fungus overwinters.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Some berries puff up hard and greenish like popcorn and never ripen. This is popcorn disease, a fungus (Ciboria carunculoides) most common in the South and on white mulberries and hybrids. No spray fixes it; you manage it by cleanup. Pick off and throw away the affected berries and clear the fallen fruit and debris under the tree, because that is where the fungus waits out the winter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Clear all fallen and affected fruit each season to break the cycle, and where popcorn disease is common, favor a red mulberry or a more resistant hybrid over the most susceptible white types.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Clean up all the fallen and affected fruit each year to stop it spreading, and where the disease is common, pick a red mulberry or a tougher hybrid instead of the most susceptible white types.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Purple stains on pavement, decking, and cars
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Purple stains all over paths and cars
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ground, pavement, decking, or vehicles under the tree are stained deep purple, and the stains track indoors. This is not a disease; it is the normal, heavy fruit drop of a productive mulberry, made worse by birds. It is almost always a siting problem. The corrective action is placement: a mature tree cannot be stopped from dropping fruit, so plant future trees, and manage this one, well away from any hard surface, and consider a weeping or dwarf form that is easier to net and harvest.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The ground, pavement, deck, or cars under the tree are stained deep purple, and it gets tracked inside. This is not a disease; it is just the normal heavy fruit drop of a productive mulberry, made worse by birds. It is really a placement problem. You cannot stop a big tree from dropping fruit, so plant future trees, and work around this one, well away from any hard surface, and think about a weeping or dwarf type that is easier to net and pick.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site mulberries away from walkways, patios, drives, and parking; for a small space choose a dwarf or weeping cultivar you can net and pick clean.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant mulberries away from paths, patios, driveways, and parking; for a small yard pick a dwarf or weeping variety you can net and pick clean.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Young mulberry seedlings appear across the yard and in beds, spread by birds eating the fruit. White mulberry in particular self-seeds readily and is considered weedy or invasive in some regions (a noxious weed in a few states). The fix is routine: pull seedlings while small, and where invasiveness is a concern choose a named, less weedy cultivar (and note that some fruitless ornamental selections were, ironically, planted to avoid exactly this).
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Little mulberry seedlings keep popping up around the yard and in beds, spread by birds eating the fruit. White mulberry especially self-seeds a lot and is considered weedy or invasive in some areas. The fix is simple: pull the seedlings while they are small, and if invasiveness is a worry where you live, choose a named, less weedy variety.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pull seedlings while small, keep fruit cleaned up, and where invasiveness is a local concern choose a named cultivar rather than a wild seedling.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pull the seedlings while small, keep the fallen fruit cleaned up, and if invasiveness is a concern where you live, plant a named variety rather than a wild seedling.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to mulberry. It is a permanent tree that occupies its site for decades and bears once each year, ripening its crop over an extended window, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual.

open_findings.summary: The NC State handbook Table 5 row that looks applicable here is "Mulberry, RED" (Morus rubra, the native species) and gives "May to June", a month earlier than our window (Jun 7 - Jul 27 in zone 7, May 31 - Jul 20 in zone 8). The row does NOT govern this crop: none of the canonical varieties is red mulberry. Illinois Everbearing, Dwarf Everbearing, Silk Hope and Oscar are everbearing M. alba x rubra hybrids, Black Beauty is M. nigra and Pakistan is a long-fruited type, all of which crop over an extended season rather than the native species' short May-June window. Trimming to the row would have made the cell wrong for every variety we recommend. Left unchanged; the species mismatch is recorded so the row is not "fixed" later.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (to -30°F and below) exceed the survival threshold of even the hardiest mulberries. Not a mulberry zone.

4.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
4.suitability_note_seasoned: The cold edge. Hardy hybrids (Illinois Everbearing, Silk Hope) and white mulberry survive and fruit here, to about -20°F; tender black and low-chill types do not. Expect a slightly later, shorter season and occasional winter dieback of less-hardy wood in severe years.
4.suitability_note_beginner: The cold edge for mulberry. Hardy varieties like Illinois Everbearing survive and fruit here, but tender black and low-chill kinds do not. The season is a bit later and shorter, and a very hard winter may nip some wood.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost is a minor risk: mulberry leafs out later than stone fruit and recovers if the new growth is nipped, so a hard late freeze rarely costs the crop.

5.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)

Mulberry blooms late, so frost is not much of a worry.
